situation:
You are nineteen, renting your first apartment, and working days at a garden center with no credit history to your name. Your auto policy with TIMBERPOINT MUTUAL INSURANCE renews in three weeks, and after a minor accident last spring the six-month premium has risen from $708 to $1,044. An insurance agent (judge) has asked to go over your choices.

Paying the $1,044 in one payment would empty the savings you keep for rent in case the garden center cuts your hours. Paying monthly costs $186, and the $12 service charge built into each installment adds $72 over the six months for nothing but the convenience of spreading it out.

CROSSCUT AUTO INSURANCE has quoted $154 a month, but that quote is state-minimum liability with no collision, so any repair to your own hatchback would come out of your pocket. You paid the car loan off last month, so the lender no longer requires collision the way a mortgage lender requires homeowners’ insurance.

The agent (judge) has also offered an extended warranty on your seven-year-old hatchback at $28 a month, a cost you can measure exactly against a breakdown that may never come. The agent (judge) wants you to compare the renewal choices and recommend one. The agent (judge) will greet you, ask to hear your ideas, and thank you after your presentation and questions.
judgeCharacterization:
You are an insurance agent (judge) at TIMBERPOINT MUTUAL INSURANCE. Business background is the same as the situation above.

You write personal auto policies and talk renewals through with customers before they lapse. You want to hear the renewal choices compared and hear which one this customer would take, in their own terms and for reasons they can state.

During the presentation you will ask the following questions:
judgeQuestions: A year from now, what will have changed because of this choice?
What would make you switch back?
